study.title: Bright and Dark
study.question: What makes music sound major or minor?
study.passage:
Guide (written for this lesson):
Major pattern: W W H W W W H (C major: C D E F G A B C).
Natural minor pattern: W H W W H W W (A minor: A B C D E F G A, all white keys).
Relative keys: A minor uses the same notes as C major but starts on A, the 6th note of C. E minor is the relative minor of G major (one sharp, F♯).
Parallel keys: C major and C minor share a tonic. C natural minor is C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C: the 3rd, 6th and 7th notes are lowered.
Chords: C major = C E G (major third C–E, four half steps); C minor = C E♭ G (minor third C–E♭, three half steps).
Activities: 1. Play C major then A minor; describe each. 2. Play "Twinkle, Twinkle" in C major, then with E♭, A♭ and B♭ (C minor). 3. Blind listening: classmates play six chords; label each major or minor. 4. Discuss: is minor always sad? (Many dance and pop songs are in minor keys.)

study.title: The Progressions Everyone Knows
study.question: Why do some chord progressions appear in so many songs?
study.passage:
Chords in C major (written for this lesson): I C, ii Dm, iii Em, IV F, V G, vi Am, vii° Bdim. Upper case = major; lower case = minor; ° = diminished.
Progression 1, I–V–vi–IV: | C | G | Am | F |. Songs that use it include "Let It Be" by the Beatles (1970) and "Don't Stop Believin'" by Journey (1981).
Progression 2, the 12-bar blues: | I | I | I | I | IV | IV | I | I | V | IV | I | I |; in C: C C C C F F C C G F C C. Bars 11–12 form the turnaround; many players use V in bar 12 to lead back to the start.
Progression 3, I–vi–IV–V: | C | Am | F | G |, a 1950s doo-wop favourite.
Activities: 1. Build each chord of C major (root, skip, skip). 2. Play I–V–vi–IV on keyboards or ukuleles (C G Am F), 4 beats per chord. 3. Play the 12-bar blues while classmates clap a shuffle rhythm. 4. Rotate: vi–IV–I–V uses the same chords from a different start. How does it feel?

study.title: Chord Detectives
study.question: How can I analyze the chords in songs I know?
study.passage:
Analysis method (written for this lesson):
1. Find the key: hum the note that sounds like "home"; that is usually the tonic.
2. Follow the bass: the lowest notes often play chord roots. Hum them and match to a keyboard.
3. Count bars: how many beats until the chord changes?
4. Label with numerals: if the key is G, then G = I, C = IV, D = V, Em = vi.
5. Look for patterns: does the verse use a different progression from the chorus? Is it a loop?
Practice set (teacher plays short excerpts or students bring school-appropriate songs): Song A: G | D | Em | C. Song B: Am | F | C | G. Song C: E | E | E | E | A | A | E | E | B | A | E | B.
Transposing: Song A in C is C | G | Am | F. Same numerals, new key.
Task: In pairs, choose one school-appropriate song, find its chord chart (from a music book or a reputable chord site), label with numerals and compare verse and chorus.
